title: How to Pixelate an Image Online Free: Censor With Pixel Blocks
description: Pixelate an image online free with ChooseTools. Block out faces, numbers and sensitive areas with clean pixelation, right in your browser, with full privacy and no watermark.

sections.heading: Pixelation Is Censorship That Stays Honest
paragraphs: Sometimes a soft blur isn't enough and a deliberate mosaic is exactly right: pixelation clearly says "obscured on purpose" while keeping the image's graphic identity. [pixelate-image:Pixelating images] is the classic way to hide a face, a number or a logo.
Newsrooms, police releases, marketplaces and school communications all rely on the mosaic look.
ChooseTools pixelates regions of images locally in your browser with block-size control over the effect.
The result is a file that follows the spirit of privacy law and editorial guidance without ever losing the context a photo carries.

sections.heading: How the Mosaic Effect Is Built
paragraphs: Pixelation works by dividing a selected area into a grid of blocks and replacing each block with a single average color from the pixels beneath it.
A coarse grid produces the heavy, unmistakable mosaic of classic censorship; a fine grid yields a grainy texture that only softens the detail.
Because the math is simple and local, the operation is instant even on high-resolution photos, and you can preview the result before committing to it.
Adjusting the block size after the selection costs nothing, so fine-tuning to the point of the image is practical rather than tedious.

sections.heading: How to Pixelate a Region of an Image
paragraphs: Censor with style and precision:
Upload the image and select the area to mask; adjust block size from a subtle grain to a heavy mosaic. Preview to confirm the content is fully hidden, then download.
Everything happens locally, so no one sees what you chose to hide or where.
Re-selecting a region is as easy as drawing the rectangle again, giving you total control over the final look before the file leaves your device.

sections.heading: Mosaic Censorship for Public Imagery
paragraphs: Broadcasting a crowd photo: mosaic the bystanders. Publishing a crime scene: mask identifiers. Selling a used car: block the plates.
The heavy mosaic look is unambiguous and timeless across print and screens.
Censoring never wipes the whole photo — only the parts the law or decency requires.
This surgical approach keeps the image useful for reporting, listings and announcements while protecting every person or detail it should not reveal.

sections.heading: Control the Blockiness for the Right Visual
paragraphs: Small blocks read as "grainy detail", large blocks as unmistakable censorship.
Matching the block size to how much must be hidden keeps the result proportionate.
The effect stays locally editable until precisely right.
For faces, a medium-to-large block hides identity clearly; for license plates and numbers, a tighter block preserves recognizability of the rest of the frame.

Because the mosaic is reconstructed from the image itself, the masked area blends naturally with the surrounding pixels rather than looking like a pasted patch — the effect stays professional in print, online and on social feeds.

sections.heading: Blur or Mosaic: Choosing the Right Mask
paragraphs: Blur softens pixels into a smooth smudge that can sometimes be partially reconstructed or visually distracting at large areas.
Pixelation breaks the region into crisp blocks that permanently remove readable detail, which is why editorial and legal workflows prefer it.
Where a preview needs to stay pleasant to the eye, a light mosaic reads cleaner than a heavy Gaussian smear.
Select the mask style that matches the story the photo must still tell after the sensitive parts disappear.

sections.heading: Private Censoring of Sensitive Files

Your decisions about public visibility happen entirely in your hands.
Whether the file is a legal exhibit, a child's school photo or an unreleased product shot, nothing about it is ever transmitted while you prepare it for sharing.

faqs.q: Can I control the size of the pixel blocks?
faqs.a: Yes. Adjust the block size along with the masked region to fine-tune how dense or coarse the mosaic appears.

faqs.q: Can I pixelate multiple areas at once?
faqs.a: Yes. Any number of regions can be masked on the same image before export.
Yes. It runs entirely in your browser with no uploads, watermarks or accounts.

faqs.q: Why choose pixelation over blur for sensitive content?
faqs.a: Pixelation removes readable detail with crisp, permanent blocks and is the standard the editorial and legal industries rely on for faces and identifiers.
